dervis-irab:1-1.t:
* Vocabulary:
(اسم): The scholars of the language disagreed about the derivation of ism (noun, "name"). The Basrans held that it derives from sumuww, which is elevation (ʿuluww), while the Kufans held that it derives from simah, which is a mark (ʿalāma). Both are sound as to meaning. It has five dialectal forms:
ism with kasra on the hamza, usm with ḍamma on it, sim with kasra on the sīn, sum with ḍamma on it, and sumā on the pattern of hudā. Now ism is one of the ten nouns whose beginnings they built on sukūn; so when they pronounce them at the start of speech they add a hamza, to avoid beginning with a sākin, because their language is free of every impediment of speech; and when the word falls in the flow of speech it needs nothing.
(الله): a proper name (ʿalam) that is applied only to the One truly worshipped, by a special right in which no other shares. According to most, it is improvised (murtajal), not derived, and Sībawayh took this view in one of his two statements; so it is not permissible to drop the alif and lām from it. It was also said that it is derived, and Sībawayh also took this view. They have two opinions on its derivation:
(a) That its origin is ilāh on the pattern fiʿāl, from their saying "aliha al-rajulu ya'lahu ilāhatan", meaning "the man worshipped, with worship". Then they dropped the hamza for lightness, because of the frequency of its occurrence and use; then the alif and lām were added for exaltation and to ward off the generality that they had adopted by calling their idols and what they worshipped "gods" (āliha) besides Allah.
(b) That its origin is lāh, and the alif and lām were then added to it; its derivation is from lāha yalīhu, "he was veiled", as if He, glory be to Him, is so named because of His concealment and His being veiled from the perception of eyes. How beautiful is the saying of the poet al-Sharīf al-Raḍī: "The wise were bewildered about His essence, the Exalted, and His attributes, because of their being veiled by the lights of majesty.
They were also bewildered about the word of majesty (lafẓ al-jalāla), as though rays reflected back to it from those lights dazzled the eyes of the discerning, and so they disagreed: is it Syriac or Arabic? A noun or an adjective? Derived, and from what is it derived? And what is its origin? Or is it not derived? A proper name or not a proper name?"
(الرَّحْمنِ): the pattern faʿlān in the language indicates a verbal attribute that carries the sense of intensity for transient attributes, like ʿaṭshān (thirsty) and gharthān (hungry). (الرَّحِيمِ): the pattern faʿīl indicates a verbal attribute that carries the sense of intensity for permanent, fixed attributes; for this reason one of the two attributes cannot dispense with the other.

* I'rab:
(بِسْمِ): a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to an omitted element. The bāʾ here is for seeking help (istiʿāna) or for attachment (ilṣāq). The implied form of the omitted element is "I begin" (abtadiʾu); so the preposition and its genitive noun are in the position of an accusative, a fronted direct object. Or it is an inceptive (ibtidāʾī), in which case the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ. Both are good. And (اللَّهِ) is muḍāf ilayhi. (الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ) are two adjectives of Allah the Exalted. The clause of the basmala is inceptive and has no grammatical position.

* Rhetoric:
The basmala contains a group of rhetorical arts:
(a) First: it is preferable that what "In the name of Allah" is attached to be an imperfect verb, because that is the original in governing and holding to the original is better, and because it indicates continuous renewal. It was omitted only because of how often the thing it is attached to circulates on the tongues. If what it is attached to were a noun, it would indicate permanence and constancy, as though beginning with the name of Allah were a perpetual obligation in every work we undertake and every word we utter.
(b) Concision (ījāz) through annexing the general to the specific; this is called ījāz qaṣr.
(c) If we make the bāʾ for seeking help, then the speech contains a figurative metaphor of the subordinate kind (istiʿāra makniyya tabaʿiyya), through likening it to a connection joining the one seeking help and the one helped; and if we make the bāʾ for attachment, then the speech contains a trope whose relation is locality (majāz ʿalāqatuhu al-maḥalliyya), as in "marartu bi-Zaydin", meaning "at a place near him", not Zayd himself.

* Benefits:
The basmala has benefits of which ignorance is not permissible, among them:
(a) Know that the basmala is a verse of Sūrat al-Ḥamd and a verse at the beginning of every sūra according to al-Shāfiʿī; according to Mālik it is not a verse in any of these; and according to Abū Ḥanīfa and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal it is a verse at the beginning of al-Fātiḥa only, and not elsewhere. The arguments for this are set out in the books of jurisprudence and exegesis, so refer to them.
(b) Nobody is described in Arabic as al-Raḥmān, with the alif and lām, except Allah the Exalted. The Arabs did describe Musaylima the Liar by it in annexed form, saying "raḥmān of al-Yamāma". One of their poets said, praising Musaylima:
سموت بالمجد يا ابن الأكرمين أبا ... وأنت غيث الورى لا زلت رحمانا
(You have risen high in glory, O son of the noblest of fathers; you are the rain of mankind; may you remain a raḥmān.)
(c) "Bismi Allāh" is written without an alif in the basmala specifically, dispensing with it because of the bāʾ of seeking help, unlike the saying of the Exalted: «اقرأ باسم ربك الذي خلق».
(d) The alif is dropped from al-Raḥmān because the alif and lām enter it.
(e) The one who says بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ is called mubasmil; this is a kind of linguistic blending (naḥt). It occurs in a poem of ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa:
لقد بسملت ليلى غداة لقيتها ... فيا حبذا ذاك الحبيب المبسمل
(Laylā said the basmala on the morning I met her; how excellent is that beloved who says the basmala!)
Like basmala is ḥawqala, when one says "lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-llāh"; hayllala, when one says "lā ilāha illā Allāh"; sabḥala, when one says "subḥān Allāh"; ḥamdala, when one says "al-ḥamdu li-llāh"; ḥayṣala and ḥayʿala, when one says "ḥayya ʿalā al-ṣalāh, ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ"; and jaʿfala, when one says "juʿiltu fidāka".
Now, blending among the Arabs is specific to relative adjectives (nisba): they take two nouns and blend a single noun from them, and then form a relative adjective from it, as they say ḥaḍramī, ʿabqasī and ʿabshī, relating to Ḥaḍramawt, ʿAbd al-Qays and ʿAbd Shams. Moreover al-Farrāʾ reported from some Arabs: "maʿī ʿasharatun fa-aḥadu-hunna lī", that is, "make them eleven". Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of "Allāhumma" is "yā Allāh, ummanā bi-khayr", that is, "direct us toward good"; so it became frequent in the speech of the Arabs. The Arabs also blended from two nouns, so it was said of al-ṣuldam (the hard, strong one) that it is from al-ṣalad (hard) and al-ṣadm (striking); and from it is Balḥārith for Banū al-Ḥārith; and perhaps al-ḥaqlad, meaning the ill-natured and heavy-spirited, is blended from al-ḥiqd (rancour) and al-thiql (heaviness). They also blended from a verb and a particle, saying al-azalī (the eternal), which is blended from "lam yazal" (he has never ceased); from a noun and a particle, saying "min min lā shayʾ talāshā"; and from two particles, as al-Khalīl said that the word (لن) is blended from lā and an, and that after its composition it took on a meaning that was not in its two components when together.
We cited these statements not because they are conclusive, for they are a matter of disagreement as you have seen, but because we took comfort in them for the sake of encouraging those who work with language to engage in blending: in it is a new wealth for our language and a facilitation of many modern expressions we lack. Blending is among the most prominent phenomena in modern foreign languages, thanks to the prefixes and suffixes attached to the root, and thanks to the flexibility they give their language when they compose a new word from two nouns, or two adjectives, or two verbs, until, once the word is composed and has been given a particular meaning, it travels on the lips in every direction. Examples of this in French are their word composed of a verb and a noun, for the handkerchief prepared for drying the hands; their word composed of two verbs, for the written permit for passage; and their word composed of two nouns, for a kind of small bird, and others.
Before the mission, Quraysh used to write at the head of their documents: «باسمك اللهمّ». Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt was the first to write «باسمك اللهم», until Islam came and بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ was revealed. Muḥammad ibn Saʿd narrated in his Ṭabaqāt that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to write as Quraysh wrote: «باسمك اللهم», until the saying of the Exalted was revealed: «وَقالَ ارْكَبُوا فِيها بِسْمِ اللَّهِ مَجْراها وَمُرْساها», and he wrote «باسم الله», until the saying of the Exalted was revealed: «قُلِ ادْعُوا اللَّهَ أَوِ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمنَ», and he wrote «باسم الله الرحمن», until the saying of the Exalted was revealed:
«إِنَّهُ مِنْ سُلَيْمانَ وَإِنَّهُ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ», and he wrote: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ.

dervis-irab:2-7.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْحَمْدُ): praise with what is beautiful and proclaiming it with the tongue; whereas shukr (thanks) is praise for a favour specifically; so between them there is a general-and-specific relation. (رَبِّ): rabb is the master, the owner, the constant, the worshipped, and the one who sets right; some added "the companion", citing as evidence the verse:
فدنا له رب الكلاب بكفّه ... بيض رهاف ريشهنّ مقزّع
(So the master of the dogs drew near to it, in his hand white, slender arrows whose feathers are scattered.)
And al-murabbī is the one who manages and directs the one he rears; it is an active participle whose alif was dropped, as bārr and barr were said. It was also said that it is a maṣdar used as a description, restricted by annexation, as in "rabb al-dār" (master of the house), from rabbahu yarubbuhu. It was also said that it is a resembling adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha) formed from a transitive verb, so it must be taken as intransitive by conversion to the pattern faʿula with ḍamma. (الْعالَمِينَ): plural of ʿālam with fatḥa on the lām; it is a sound masculine plural of rational beings by predominance (taghlīban), but what is meant is all created beings. For this reason the grammarians included it among what is attached to the sound masculine plural. The subtle point in it is that this word is not applied among the Arabs to every existing being, such as stone and dust, but only to every aggregate whose members are distinguished by attributes that bring them close to the rational being, whose plural form it was given, even though it is not of them. So one says: the world of man, the world of animals, the world of plants. And ʿālam has no singular, either from its own wording or from another, because it is a plural of different things. (الدِّينِ): requital; "the Day of Dīn" is the Day of Requital. From it is the saying of the Arabs: «كما تدين تدان» ("as you requite, you will be requited"), and the saying of the poet:
ولم يبق سوى العدوا ... ن دناهم كما دانوا
(Nothing remained but hostility; we requited them as they had requited.)
Dīn is also obedience, as in the saying of the Exalted «في دين الملك», and dīn is also religion (milla). Al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī said:
تقول إذا درأت لها وضيني ... أهذا دينه أبدا وديني
(She says, when I shifted her girth: "Is this always his religion and my religion?")
(الصِّراطَ): the clear road and the way. Jarīr said:
أمير المؤمنين على صراط ... إذا اعوجّ الموارد مستقيم
(The Commander of the Believers is on a path that is straight when the watering-places are crooked.)
There are four dialectal forms of ṣirāṭ: sirāṭ with sīn, from saraṭa al-shayʾa, "he swallowed it", the road being called sirāṭ because people run along it as a swallowed thing passes down; ṣirāṭ; with a pure zāy; and with ṣād pronounced with an admixture of zāy (ishmām). All of these have been recited. It is treated as masculine or feminine, and the masculine is more frequent.

* I'rab:
(الْحَمْدُ): mubtadaʾ. (لِلَّهِ): a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to an omitted khabar. (رَبِّ): an adjective of Allah, or a substitute (badal) for it. (الْعالَمِينَ): muḍāf ilayhi, genitive, and the sign of its genitive case is yāʾ in place of kasra because it is attached to the sound masculine plural. (الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ): two adjectives of Allah the Exalted as well. (مالِكِ): a fourth adjective of Allah. It was also read malik ("king"), and there is a subtle difference between them: mālik is the one who has milk (ownership), with kasra on the mīm, and malik is the one who has mulk (kingship), with ḍamma on it. The grammarians said that malik is more laudatory than mālik, because a mālik may not be a king whereas a king is necessarily a mālik. The plural of malik is amlāk and mulūk, and the plural of mālik is milāk and mālikūn. (يَوْمِ الدِّينِ): muḍāf ilayhi. (إِيَّاكَ): a detached pronoun in the position of an accusative, a fronted direct object, for the sake of restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ). (نَعْبُدُ): a nominative imperfect verb, its agent a latent pronoun obligatorily implied, its implied form being "we". (وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ): conjoined to «إياك نعبد»; and نَسْتَعِينُ is a nominative imperfect verb, and it is a hollow (muʿtall ajwaf) verb, the original being nastaʿwinu; the kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so it was moved to the ʿayn, and the wāw turned into yāʾ because of the kasra before it, giving nastaʿīnu. (اهْدِنَا): an imperative verb, indeclinable by dropping of the weak letter, and here it has the meaning of supplication; and nā is an attached pronoun in the position of an accusative, a direct object, and its agent is a latent pronoun obligatorily implied, its implied form being "you". (الصِّراطَ): a second direct object, or accusative by removal of the preposition, because hadā is not transitive except to one object and is made transitive to the second by lām, as in the saying of the Exalted: «يهدي للتي هي أقوم», or by ilā, as in the saying of the Exalted: «وإنك لتهدى إلى صراط مستقيم»; but extension (ittisāʿ) prevailed in it, so some made it transitive to two. Some of the witty composed verses that include the verbs which are transitive to one object and to the second through a preposition, namely:
تعدى من الافعال طورا بنفسه ... وحينا بحرف الجر للثان ما ترى
دعا في الندا سمّى كذا كنى ... وزوجه واستغفر اختار غيرا
أمرت صدقت الوعد كلت وزنته ... عفا وهدى منّى كذا سأل اذكرا
(Of the verbs, some are at times transitive by themselves and at times by a preposition to the second, as you see: daʿā in calling, sammā, likewise kannā, and zawwaja, and istaghfara, ikhtāra, ghayra; amartu, ṣaddaqtu, the promise, kiltu, waznuhu; ʿafā and hadā, mannā, likewise saʾala; remember them.)
[Translator's note: the verse text is given as in the source and is evidently corrupt in places; the translation above only lists the verb names.] Altogether they are sixteen verbs. (الْمُسْتَقِيمَ): an adjective of ṣirāṭ, and it is a weak verb whose middle radical is wāw, the original being mustaqwim; the kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so it was moved to the qāf, and the wāw turned into yāʾ because of the kasra before it. (صِراطَ): an exact substitute (badal muṭābiq) for «الصراط». (الَّذِينَ): a relative noun, muḍāf ilayhi, in the position of genitive. (أَنْعَمْتَ): a past verb, indeclinable on sukūn because it is attached to a vowelled pronoun of the nominative, and the tāʾ is an attached pronoun in the position of the nominative, an agent; and the clause «أنعمت» has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila of the relative. (عَلَيْهِمْ): a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to «أنعمت». (غَيْرِ): a substitute for the pronoun in «عليهم», or for «الذين», or an adjective of «الذين»; a full discussion of ghayr will come in the section of benefits. (الْمَغْضُوبِ): muḍāf ilayhi. (عَلَيْهِمْ): a preposition and its genitive noun, in the position of nominative, a deputy agent of «المغضوب», because it is a passive participle. (وَلَا): the wāw is a conjunction and lā is redundant, to reinforce the meaning of negation, which is the negation contained in ghayr; and this redundancy is regular. (الضَّالِّينَ): conjoined to «المغضوب عليهم», genitive, and the sign of its genitive case is yāʾ because it is a sound masculine plural.

* Rhetoric:
This sūra, despite its brevity, contains several kinds of rhetoric, which we set out below:
1- The clause «الحمد لله» is a statement (khabar), but it is used to originate praise; and the benefit of the nominal clause is the permanence, continuity and constancy of praise.
2- In the saying «إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين» there is the art of fronting (taqdīm): the pronoun was fronted to restrict worship and seeking help to Allah alone. Worship was put before seeking help because seeking help is its fruit. The repetition of «إياك» with the second verb indicates that each of worship and seeking help is intended in itself, so neither of them necessarily implies the other. And because the kāf that accompanies iyyā is the very kāf that would have been attached to the verb, I mean to the verb «نعبد», had it been placed after the verb, and it is a pronominal reference to the addressee that is accusative to the verb, it was multiplied through iyyā when fronted, and the more eloquent course was to repeat it with each verb.
3- In the saying «لله» there is the art of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), to show that all praises are specific to Him; and likewise through the annexation in the saying «مالك يوم الدين», because owners and possessions disappear from all but Him on that Day.
4- In this sūra there is the art of shifting (iltifāt), from the wording of the third person to the wording of address, and from the wording of address to the wording of the third person. The aim of this art is to refresh the vigour of the mind, following their manner of expression; and because, when He had praised Allah with what He is worthy of and applied to Him those great attributes, it became fitting to ask for His help after having prepared for it with what justifies the request, and He, the Exalted, is worthy of answering; and to give notice that the first thing to which servants should resort in asking for what they need is His worship and the acknowledgment of the sublime attributes of divinity. He said «صراط الذين أنعمت عليهم» and was explicit in address when He mentioned favour, then said «غير المغضوب عليهم» and removed the wording of anger from Himself, out of tenderness and gentleness; and this is the utmost that eloquence reaches. These are the levels of iltifāt in this sūra:
(a) He turned from the third person to address in His saying «إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين» after His saying «الحمد لله رب العالمين», because praise is lower in rank than worship; do you not see that you may envy your equal and not worship him? Since the case is like this, the wording of praise was used because it occupies the middle ground with the third person in the statement, and He did not say "al-ḥamdu laka".
(b) When it came to worship, which is the utmost of acts of obedience, He said «إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين», addressing Him in worship so as to be explicit about it, and drawing near to Him, mighty and majestic, by ending at a limited number of them.
(c) The end of the sūra came in a similar way: He said «صراط الذين أنعمت عليهم», being explicit in address when He mentioned favour, then said «غير المغضوب عليهم», conjoined to the first, because the first is the place of drawing near to Allah by mentioning His favours and bounties; and when it came to mentioning anger, the wording turned aside from mentioning the one who is angry: favour was ascribed to Him in wording, and the wording of anger was removed from Him, out of tenderness and gentleness.
(d) He used the nūn of the plural in «نعبد» and «نستعين» though the speaker is one, because it is reported in the Sharīʿa that whoever sells different kinds of goods in a single deal, and a defect then appears to the buyer in some of them, may choose between returning all or keeping it, and may not split the deal by returning the defective and keeping the sound. Here, when the worshipper saw that his worship was deficient and defective, he did not present it to Allah on its own, but inclined to add the worship of all worshippers to it and presented everything as a complete deal, hoping that his worship would be accepted within it, since the whole is never altogether rejected, because part of it is accepted; and returning the defective and keeping the sound is a splitting of the deal, which He, glory be to Him, forbade His servants, and which does not befit His great generosity and all-embracing bounty. So acceptance of the whole remained.
5- Since the opening of the Qur'an with al-Fātiḥa is being mentioned, we mention this art in al-Fātiḥa: it is barāʿat al-istihlāl (excellence of the opening), one of the most delicate and graceful of the arts of rhetoric. Its definition is that the speaker begins his speech with what points to the intended purpose without explicit statement, but with a subtle hint, an allusion either distant or near. Istihlāl originally means raising the voice, and the new moon is called hilāl because people raise their voices on seeing it. Among its examples in poetry is the saying of Abū Tammām at the opening of his ode "The Conquest of ʿAmmūriya":
السّيف أصدق أنباء من الكتب ... في حدّه الحدّ بين الجدّ والّلعب
(The sword is more truthful in its tidings than the books; in its edge lies the boundary between earnestness and play.)
He opened his ode with mention of the sword, which holds a very near allusion to the subject for which the ode was composed. Abū al-Ṭayyib was famous for the excellence of his openings, among the finest of which is his saying:
أتراها لكثرة العشّاق ... تحسب الدّمع خلقة في المآقي
(Does she, because of the great number of lovers, think that tears are a natural feature of the eye-corners?)
He alluded to the subject of his ode, which is love poetry, with a gracefulness enhanced by the novelty of the idea in her reckoning tears a natural feature of the eye-corners, giving beauty and charm.
6- Explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya) in the saying «اهدنا الصراط المستقيم»: the true religion is likened to the straight path, in which there is not the slightest deviation that might take it out of the bounds of straightness, because the straight line is the shortest distance between two points. The point of resemblance between them is that Allah, glory be to Him, though exalted above places, the servant who seeks to arrive must needs traverse distances and meet with afflictions, so that arrival and meeting may be honoured.
7- Explanation after vagueness (al-tafsīr baʿda al-ibhām), in His saying: «صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ».
8- Rhymed prose (tasjīʿ) in «الرحيم» and «المستقيم», and in «نستعين» and «الضالين»; tasjīʿ is the agreement of two words in pattern and rhyme-letter (rawiyy).

* Benefits:
This sūra contains countless benefits, and we shall mention those of them that are important to know:
1- The alif and lām in «الحمد» are for the genus, according to the sounder view, because the reality of praises belongs to Allah the Exalted.
2- This sūra was named «al-Fātiḥa» because it is the beginning of the Qur'an and the excellence of its opening, and it is called «Umm al-Kitāb» because it contains lofty ideals, and it is Meccan according to the sounder view. Among its names are al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, al-Shāfiya, al-Ruqya, al-Kanz, al-Asās, and others.
3- Ghayr: the word ghayr is always masculine singular; but if a feminine is meant by it, it is permitted to put its verb, which is predicated of it, in the feminine: you say "qāmat ghayru Hind" meaning a woman. It is originally an adjective with the sense of an active participle, and it denotes difference, which is why it does not become definite by annexation. It may also be used for exception, by analogy with illā, just as it is described by illā by analogy with it. It is one of the words that are always annexed, in wording or in implication, so putting the alif and lām on it is an error.
4- The end of al-Fātiḥa is «ولا الضّالّين»; as for the word āmīn, it is not part of it, nor of the Qur'an at all. It is a noun meaning "answer" (istajib), and it is a sunna to conclude al-Fātiḥa with it. It has two forms: lengthened and shortened. Abū Nuwās said, with the lengthening:
صلى الإله على لوط وشيعته ... أبا عبيدة قل بالله: آمينا
(May the Deity bless Lot and his followers; Abū ʿUbayda, say by Allah: Āmīn!)
And another said, with the shortening:
تباعد مني فطحل إذ دعوته ... أمين فزاد الله ما بيننا بعدا
(Faṭḥal kept far from me when I called him, "Amīn"; may Allah increase the distance between us.)
5- It may be said: the believers are already guided, so what is the meaning of asking for guidance? The answer is that what is asked is steadfastness in guidance or an increase of it. That some people have not been guided does not remove it from being guidance: the sun is the sun even if the blind man does not see it, and honey is honey even if the sick man with the bitter mouth does not find its taste. The complete failure is for the one who is thirsty while the water overflows, the one who remains in darkness while the full moon shines, and the one who is foul while the good is present.
6- The most probable view is that al-Fātiḥa was the first complete sūra revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to make it the beginning of the Qur'an, and consensus was reached on that. The revelation of the beginning of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq, «اقرأ باسم ربك الذي خلق», is regarded as a preparation for the summary and detailed revelation, so it does not conflict with al-Fātiḥa's being the first sūra of the Qur'an. Al-Suyūṭī mentioned in al-Itqān that the first verses of the Qur'an to be revealed were «اقرأ باسم ربك», «يا أيها المدثر» and Sūrat al-Fātiḥa.
